title: Microprocessor scaling
summary: Fifty years of CPUs as five measures over time; Moore's law (transistor count doubling) and Dennard scaling (constant power density) and where the second one ended.

concepts.label: Microprocessor
concepts.description: A CPU on one chip; each point is a processor at its year of introduction.

children.label: Transistor count
children.description: Transistors on the die, in thousands.

children.label: Thermal design power
children.description: Typical power in W: the heat the cooler must remove.

children.label: Supply voltage
children.description: Core voltage V; dynamic power goes as V². It stopped falling in the mid-2000s.

children.label: Die area
children.description: Chip area in mm²; with power it gives power density, Dennard's invariant.

concepts.label: Scaling law
concepts.description: Empirical regularities of chip improvement over time.

children.label: Moore's law
children.description: Transistor count doubles about every two years (Moore 1975).

facts.text: Moore's 1965 paper predicted a doubling every year, revised to every two years in 1975.

children.label: Dennard scaling
children.description: Shrinking a MOSFET by k lowers voltage and capacitance by k, so power density stays constant while the clock rises (Dennard et al. 1974).

facts.text: Dennard et al., Design of ion-implanted MOSFETs with very small physical dimensions, IEEE JSSC 1974.

children.label: Leakage current
children.description: Subthreshold leakage grows exponentially as threshold voltage falls; it is why voltage scaling stopped.

concepts.label: Structural break
concepts.description: The year a trend changes slope, found by the minimum two-line SSE and tested with a Chow F-test.
